passages.text: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) is commonly used in both supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL), often under similar optimizer settings. Yet, how the different dynamics of the two stages manifest in the low-rank increment that LoRA optimizes remains unclear. Tracking the singular spectrum and subspaces of LoRA updates on mathematical reasoning tasks, we find that RL concentrates the spectrum at every learning rate, while SFT expands it at moderate learning rates; moreover, RL rotates the singular subspaces much faster than SFT at small learning rates. Interpolating between SFT and RL one ingredient at a time, we pinpoint group-mean baseline subtraction as the source of both contrasts. A quadratic multi-index model updated via LoRA unveils the underlying mechanism: group-mean baseline subtraction tilts the balance between two competing forces, coherent fitting and gradient noise, toward spectral concentration and faster subspace rotation, while forcing the risk-favorable learning rate to be low. Guided by these dynamics, we tailor LoRA updates to each stage: in SFT, we flatten the spectrum of the full update to spread adaptation across singular directions, whereas in RL, we flatten the part of the update outside the current LoRA increment span to promote subspace rotation. Experiments on mathematical reasoning tasks across multiple models show that the respective configurations for SFT and RL yield the best performance among the compared methods in most evaluated settings.

In SFT, we flatten the singular spectrum of the full update of the factor so that the adaptation is distributed more evenly across singular directions; whereas in RL, we flatten only the component of the update orthogonal to the current left singular subspace of Δ ​ W t \Delta W_{t} , which promotes subspace rotation while leaving the within-subspace component unchanged. The resulting configurations achieve dominating downstream performance across most evaluated models and tasks.

passages.section: Differences between supervised and reinforcement fine-tuning.
passages.text: Prior work has characterized differences between SFT and RL at the output, representation, and parameter levels. At the output level, empirical studies report stronger out-of-distribution performance under RL than SFT [ 18 , 5 ] . Subsequent work further highlights the dependence of SFT generalization on optimization, data quality, and model capability [ 29 ] . Beyond performance, studies examine the diversity of generated outputs: RLHF reduces overall response diversity relative to SFT [ 18 ] , while analyses distinguishing correct and incorrect reasoning trajectories find that SFT expands the former and RL compresses the latter [ 21 ] . Moreover, a line of work examines how changes in the model’s output distribution during fine-tuning relate to the preservation of pretrained capabilities. These studies illustrate how on-policy RL can better preserve distributional modes associated with prior knowledge than SFT [ 4 ] , and link RL’s better retention to an implicit preference for output distributions closer to that of the initial model in KL divergence [ 34 ] . At the hidden representation level, Shi et al. [35] find that SFT rapidly introduces specialized features that stabilize early, whereas RL induces more restrained but continually evolving feature changes.

passages.section: Differences between supervised and reinforcement fine-tuning.
passages.text: At the parameter update level, studies report greater sparsity in parameter updates under RL than SFT [ 24 ] . Comparisons of update vectors across tasks reveal large absolute cosine similarities under SFT, whereas RL updates are nearly orthogonal [ 50 ] . Spectral analyses of the weight matrices further show smaller changes from the pretrained spectra and principal subspaces under RLVR than SFT [ 49 ] . Our work also compares spectral and subspace dynamics under SFT and RL. In contrast, we focus on the LoRA update matrix itself, track how its spectral concentration and subspace rotation vary with learning rate and training step, interpolate between SFT and RL through intermediate training settings to identify where these differences arise, and use these findings to guide the choice of optimizer configurations for LoRA in each paradigm.

In this work, we identify distinct spectral and subspace dynamics of LoRA under SFT and RL. Our experiments show that RL effective rank consistently decreases during training across the learning rates considered, while for models that benefit from SFT, the growth of effective rank accompanies better SFT performance at intermediate learning rates. In addition to this difference in spectral dynamics, RL exhibits faster subspace rotation than SFT at small learning rates, with the gap narrowing as the learning rate increases. Controlled comparisons identify group-mean baseline subtraction as a key source of these differences. Using a multi-index model, our theoretical framework analyzes how baseline subtraction changes coherent fitting and feedback from gradient noise, jointly shaping effective rank, subspace rotation, and learning-rate preferences in prediction risk. These insights guide the choice of two dynamics-informed configurations for LoRA optimization, tailored to the distinct training dynamics of SFT and RL. Both configurations achieve the highest reported mean accuracy in most evaluated settings.

Existing dynamic-rank methods mainly focus on capacity allocation, leaving unresolved whether the current adaptation space is sufficient for the task. We characterize the first-order information boundary of standard factor gradients, showing that their unobservable subspace coincides with the normal space of the low-rank manifold. Thus, factor gradients alone cannot distinguish under-optimization within the current space from task-relevant directions beyond its first-order reach. This motivates a geometric view of rank evolution, where tangent information optimizes existing degrees of freedom and the normal spectrum quantifies the value of new ones. Under a local quadratic model, we show that leading normal singular directions yield the locally optimal rank expansion, with spectral energy determining its gain. Building on this characterization, we propose GEAR, which turns the tangent–normal decomposition into rank evolution through tangent-space optimization, matrix-free normal-spectrum estimation for rank expansion, and task-induced geometric initialization. Across language and vision benchmarks, GEAR achieves the best average performance in all evaluated settings with substantially fewer trainable parameters. On LLaMA3-8B, it raises the average commonsense score from 86.61 to 88.45 while reducing trainable parameters from 42.0M to 14.4M.

Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) has become a prevailing approach to adapting large pretrained models by updating only a small fraction of task-specific parameters ( Ding et al., 2023b ) . Among PEFT methods, LoRA represents the weight increment as a low-rank matrix, Δ ​ W = B ​ A \Delta W=BA , where A ∈ ℝ r × m A\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times m} and B ∈ ℝ n × r B\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r} , reducing the number of trainable parameters from n ​ m nm to r ⁡ ( n + m ) r(n+m) ( Hu et al., 2022 ) . While r r therefore directly controls the adaptation budget, it also determines the local first-order update space accessible under the low-rank constraint ( Vandereycken, 2013 ) . Rank thus governs both adaptation capacity and which task-induced directions can be expressed. Since these requirements vary across layers and throughout training, a uniform fixed rank is unlikely to match the evolving structure of task demand, motivating dynamic-rank adaptation.

Most dynamic-rank methods still treat rank primarily as a capacity-allocation variable. AdaLoRA, for example, reallocates a prescribed rank budget across weight matrices according to the importance of individual singular components ( Zhang et al., 2023 ) , while DyLoRA trains nested low-rank structures to support inference at multiple truncation ranks ( Valipour et al., 2023 ) . Although these methods substantially improve the flexibility of rank adaptation, their rank decisions are primarily derived from the capacity or structure already represented by the current adapter. They therefore characterize what the current low-rank space uses, but provide no direct criterion for determining whether task-relevant descent directions remain missing outside that space. This leaves a more fundamental question unresolved: Is the current adaptation space locally sufficient to express task-relevant descent directions, or must its rank expand to make such directions first-order accessible?

Much less is understood when parameters and gradients are naturally matrix-valued, as in Transformers and convolutional networks. Recently, Singular-Spectrum-Based Optimization (SSBO) methods, such as Muon [ 16 ] , Shampoo [ 13 ] , and SOAP [ 49 ] , have attracted growing attention for their ability to preserve the matrix structure of neural network updates. Among them, Muon has garnered the most interest due to its exceptional efficiency in large language model (LLM) training. Muon also has a relatively simple implementation: it orthogonalizes a matrix-valued momentum before applying the update, yielding geometry-aware descent directions [ 28 , 15 ] . Despite the promise of these SSBO methods, both their theory and implementation remain largely confined to centralized training in the literature, leaving open the question of how they should be designed and analyzed in distributed settings.

However, developing SSBO-based methods for distributed learning is highly non-trivial due to several technical challenges. First , the nonlinear spectral mapping does not commute with distributed aggregation. Averaging locally transformed spectral directions is generally not equivalent to applying the spectral map after aggregating the underlying momentum estimates, which can introduce systematic bias. Second , data heterogeneity and noisy gradient estimates further exacerbate this nonlinearity challenge. In distributed stochastic training, deviations in the momentum estimators are coupled with the nonlinear spectral mapping and can lead to directional errors, suggesting that the matrix-valued estimator should be carefully controlled before applying the spectral map. Third , practical Muon-style implementations typically replace exact orthogonalization with finite-step Newton–Schulz (NS) iterations. The resulting approximation error must therefore be explicitly accounted for in the convergence analysis. Fourth , synchronizing full matrix-valued momentum variables incurs substantial communication cost. This high communication cost motivates low-rank communication, whose additional approximation error must also be carefully controlled. passages.text: Muon has recently emerged as a promising optimizer for pretraining large language models, offering a speedup over AdamW in minimizing pretraining loss. However, it remains unclear whether Muon’s advantage persists after fine-tuning. In this paper, we study the downstream behavior of Muon and AdamW and uncover a surprising trend: beyond a sufficiently large pretraining data budget, AdamW outperforms Muon after fine-tuning. Moreover, as model size increases, AdamW overtakes Muon at progressively smaller pretraining token–parameter ratios. To explain this reversal, we view fine-tuning as a perturbation of the outputs and introduce the margin-to-spread ratio, which measures how far the correct logit lies above the wrong ones relative to how widely the wrong logits are spread. In language models, Muon has the larger margin-to-spread ratio at small data budgets and AdamW at large ones, mirroring the fine-tuning trend. In a linear associative memory, we prove that after one update the margin-to-spread ratio of gradient descent gains on that of Muon as the data budget grows, and simulations show that this trend persists after extended training. Catherine Li ∗ Jingchu Gai ∗ Andrej Risteski Jacob Mitchell Springer † Aditi Raghunathan † Carnegie Mellon University {catheri4, jgai}@andrew.cmu.edu

We test whether the budget trend predicted by Section 4.2 also appears in real language models, beyond the assumptions used in our theoretical analysis. Setup. We evaluate the AdamW and Muon models trained in Section 3 , spanning five model sizes, on held-out DCLM text. We compute the MSR at each token position and report the median over correctly predicted positions. At each position, h h and κ \kappa are the mean and standard deviation of the margins between the correct next-token logit and all other vocabulary logits. We use the median to reduce sensitivity to outliers; Section 4.1 instead uses the mean margin divided by the square root of the mean variance. Experimental Result. Figure 5 plots the MSR for the three model sizes with the widest budget ranges, from 30M to 100M. Muon has a larger MSR at small data budgets, while AdamW has a larger MSR at sufficiently large budgets. As the budget grows, the difference between AdamW’s and Muon’s MSRs increases, and the ratio of AdamW’s MSR to Muon’s crosses one. This shift toward AdamW is consistent with the theoretical budget trend and parallels the reversal in relative robustness to fine-tuning observed in Section 3 . (b) The MSR ratio ρ AdamW / ρ Muon \rho^{\mathrm{AdamW}}/\rho^{\mathrm{Muon}} crosses one as the budget grows, at every model size.

The MSR and fine-tuning crossovers do not necessarily appear at exactly the same budget, since the learning–forgetting tradeoff also depends on pretraining loss. Nevertheless, the MSR captures the direction of the observed shift and connects our theoretical analysis to the behavior of trained language models. Remark. We summarize the analysis of this section and relate MSR to other metrics used to predict post-training. • Takeaway. In a linear associative memory, we prove that after one update the ratio ρ GD / ρ Muon \rho^{\mathrm{GD}}/\rho^{\mathrm{Muon}} of the two optimizers’ MSRs increases with the data budget ( Section 4.2 ). Simulations of many training steps show that the same trend persists after extended training ( Section 4.2 ). • Extension: Relation of MSR to Other Metrics Predicting Post-Training. Other work predicts forgetting after post-training with different metrics. For example, Springer et al. (2025) show that the loss increase after adding Gaussian noise to the pretrained weights tracks how much a model degrades under fine-tuning. In Appendix B , we show that MSR is connected to this robustness to Gaussian perturbations: in the linear memory, a larger MSR provably guarantees that more competitors stay ranked below the correct answer after the perturbation ( Section B.2.1 ), and in both language models and the linear memory, MSR is strongly correlated with perturbation robustness ( Section B.2.2 ).

Muon. Muon, an optimizer introduced by Jordan et al. (2024) , has recently shown strong empirical performance for pretraining LLMs, challenging AdamW’s dominance as the status-quo optimizer. Recent work has sought to explain Muon’s pretraining advantage through analyses of simplified theoretical models, associative memory, convergence behavior, and loss landscape geometry ( Kim et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026 ; Sato et al., 2025 ; Su, 2025 ; Shen et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2026a ) . Another line of work investigates the training dynamics of Muon, finding that it learns data components more uniformly than AdamW ( Vasudeva et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026b ; Dragutinović et al., 2026 ) , while also characterizing the implicit biases of Muon ( Fan et al., 2025 ; Dragutinović et al., 2026 ) . Yet fewer works have examined the downstream consequences of Muon. Ruan et al. (2026) compare Muon and AdamW after fine-tuning; they find that for small data regimes, Muon outperforms AdamW, consistent with our findings. We show that this advantage does not generalize across pretraining data scale; after a sufficiently large pretraining data budget, the trend reverses, and AdamW outperforms Muon.

Muon versus AdamW on pretraining loss. Muon has been reported to reach lower pretraining loss than AdamW for the same compute across a wide range of settings ( Liu et al., 2025 ; Essential AI et al., 2025 ; Mehta et al., 2025 ) , and frontier models have since been pretrained with Muon or its variants ( Kimi Team, 2025 ; GLM-4.5 Team et al., 2025 ) . The size of this advantage depends on scale: under controlled tuning, Muon’s speedup over AdamW shrinks as model size and data grow, and Muon is overtaken by other matrix-based optimizers at large data-to-model ratios ( Wen et al., 2026b ; Wen et al., 2026a ) . All of these works measure pretraining loss. Optimizers can also reach qualitatively different solutions rather than faster or slower routes to the same minimum ( Pascanu et al., 2025 ) ; we ask whether these differences matter after fine-tuning.

Catastrophic forgetting. Catastrophic forgetting, the degradation of previously learned knowledge during subsequent training, remains a central challenge in deep learning ( Goodfellow et al., 2014 ) . Numerous approaches have been proposed to mitigate catastrophic forgetting, including regularization-based methods ( Kirkpatrick et al., 2017 ; Zenke et al., 2017 ; Aljundi et al., 2018 ) , replay techniques ( Shin et al., 2017 ) , gradient projection methods ( Lopez-Paz & Ranzato, 2017 ; Chaudhry et al., 2019 ) , and optimization-based approaches ( Watts et al., 2026 ) . Our learning–forgetting tradeoff is an instance of the stability–plasticity dilemma, with fine-tuning performance capturing plasticity and knowledge retention capturing stability ( Lopez-Paz & Ranzato, 2017 ) . We study forgetting as an intrinsic property of the pretrained checkpoint, rather than as a consequence of the fine-tuning algorithm. Specifically, we investigate how optimization choices during pretraining shape downstream forgetting, showing that Muon and AdamW induce different learning–forgetting tradeoffs.

Catastrophic forgetting, the degradation of previously learned knowledge during subsequent training, remains a central challenge in deep learning ( Goodfellow et al., 2014 ) . Numerous approaches have been proposed to mitigate catastrophic forgetting, including regularization-based methods ( Kirkpatrick et al., 2017 ; Zenke et al., 2017 ; Aljundi et al., 2018 ) , replay techniques ( Shin et al., 2017 ) , gradient projection methods ( Lopez-Paz & Ranzato, 2017 ; Chaudhry et al., 2019 ) , and optimization-based approaches ( Watts et al., 2026 ) . Our learning–forgetting tradeoff is an instance of the stability–plasticity dilemma, with fine-tuning performance capturing plasticity and knowledge retention capturing stability ( Lopez-Paz & Ranzato, 2017 ) . We study forgetting as an intrinsic property of the pretrained checkpoint, rather than as a consequence of the fine-tuning algorithm. Specifically, we investigate how optimization choices during pretraining shape downstream forgetting, showing that Muon and AdamW induce different learning–forgetting tradeoffs.

passages.text: Zeroth-order (ZO) optimization estimates descent directions from function values alone, which removes the activation storage required by backpropagation and makes it attractive for memory-efficient fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs). Existing low-rank ZO methods either parameterize the additive update through Euclidean factors with a non-unique representation, or restrict each finite-difference direction to be low-rank. In this work, we propose to constrain each additive update block to a fixed-rank matrix manifold while keeping the pretrained weights frozen, so the learned update remains rank-constrained throughout fine-tuning. On this geometry, we build a Riemannian ZO gradient estimator that projects a random matrix onto the tangent space, normalizes it to correct the scale mismatch induced by projection, and further propose Zeroth-order Riemannian Gradient Descent (ZO-RGD) and its smoothed variant, ZO-RGD-S. We show that the ambient finite difference matches its retracted counterpart, the normalized estimator recovers the Riemannian gradient in expectation, and ZO-RGD converges under trajectory-regularity conditions. Experiments on LLM fine-tuning tasks show that the proposed algorithms are competitive with strong forward-only baselines across model families and tasks, with gains in several settings.

Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable success across a wide range of domains ( Brown et al., 2020 ; Achiam et al., 2023 ) . Fine-tuning these models on downstream tasks is crucial for their practical deployment. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) techniques such as low-rank adaptation (LoRA) ( Hu et al., 2022 ) have emerged as a practical solution, training low-rank updates while keeping pretrained weights frozen ( Hu et al., 2022 ; Liu et al., 2024a ; Zhang et al., 2023 ; Hayou et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2024a ) . However, first-order optimization still incurs substantial memory overhead from storing activations for backpropagation, especially in long-context settings where activations dominate memory. To enhance memory efficiency, zeroth-order (ZO) fine-tuning methods ( Malladi et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2024 ) estimate descent directions from function values without backpropagated gradients, avoiding the activation storage required by backward passes ( Spall, 1992 ) .

Recent low-rank ZO fine-tuning methods combine these two directions by restricting the finite-difference search through low-rank perturbations, adapter factors, gradient estimators, or random subspaces ( Chen et al., 2025 ; Yu et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2024b ; Song and Li, 2026 ) . Factor-based approaches constrain the learned update through adapter coordinates, whereas low-rank perturbation methods constrain individual ZO steps. These two branches of methods differ in the way of constructing low-rank additive update matrices when optimizing a fixed-rank update matrix. We formulate forward-only LLM fine-tuning as optimization of persistent additive updates on fixed-rank matrix manifolds, so that the rank constraint is imposed on the optimization state rather than on individual ZO steps. ZO-RGD estimates the Riemannian gradient from two forward passes with normalized tangent finite differences and retracts each update onto the manifold. In this paper, we study continuous-time dynamics that applies a finite number of Newton–Schulz iterations to the normalized matrix gradient (Muon). We show that the number of Newton–Schulz steps can change the rank selected during the early stages of training and allow the resulting trajectory to bypass the first nonzero stationary point approached by gradient flow. Under an additional residual-inertia condition, we prove that bypass occurs for all sufficiently large finite Newton–Schulz depths and provide an explicit sufficient threshold. We also construct an example in which the bypass threshold is four. † † shortheadings: Finite-Depth Newton–Schulz Dynamics / Long † † firstpage: 1 † † heading: 2026 1–

Gradient-based training of factorized models from small initialization can exhibit incremental learning, with different components becoming appreciable at successive stages ( Saxe et al., 2014 ; Jacot et al., 2021 ; Li et al., 2021 ; Berthier, 2023 ; Jin et al., 2023 ) . In matrix factorization, this behavior can take the form of dominant directions being learned first, followed by weaker directions that increase the effective rank of the predictor. The trajectory may consequently pass near intermediate low-rank stationary points. Related analyses of homogeneous networks describe directional convergence near the origin and saddle points, as well as the subsequent trajectory toward the first saddle after escape ( Kumar and Haupt, 2024 ; Kumar and Haupt, 2025 ) . A complementary approach studies training dynamics in high-dimensional limits, extracting effective structure from the evolving parameters or deriving dynamical mean-field descriptions of gradient flow ( Martin et al., 2024 ; Martin et al., 2026 ) . Related work on feature learning and the distinction from lazy training provides another perspective on how different directions become accessible during optimization ( Chizat et al., 2019 ; Dandi et al., 2024 ) . Since Newton–Schulz iterations amplify small singular values of the normalized gradient, a natural question is whether a finite increase in the number of iterations can make weaker directions emerge early enough to change which stationary points the trajectory approaches. Answering this question requires tracking both singular-value amplification and the coupled evolution of different directions, as the gradient and its singular subspaces evolve with the factorized parameters.

Another question concerns the extent to which small-initialization asymptotics can determine the subsequent training trajectory. Under suitable structural conditions, gradient flow admits a precise description in which the initialization scale can be used to reverse-engineer the full training dynamics, leading also to a characterization of time-dependent implicit regularization ( Berthier, 2023 ) . For finite-depth Newton–Schulz dynamics, the nonlinear matrix iteration prevents this reconstruction argument from carrying over directly. Although the dynamics can be analyzed in a small neighborhood of the origin, the resulting local description does not by itself determine the trajectory after leaving that neighborhood. This creates two distinct dynamical scales: the entrance dynamics near the origin and the subsequent evolution away from it. Establishing how the entrance dynamics are transmitted to the later trajectory is one of the main results of this paper.

Following the framework of Li et al. (2021) , which characterizes the first nonzero stationary point selected by gradient flow under suitable assumptions, we study the evolution from small initialization through the first stationary point encountered after escape. This allows us to compare the stationary points approached by gradient descent and by finite-depth Newton–Schulz dynamics. Under an additional structural assumption, we establish a sufficient large-depth guarantee: for all sufficiently large spectral depths, the selected Newton–Schulz continuation approaches a first stationary point whose loss is strictly smaller than that of the first stationary point selected by gradient descent. For smaller depths, our results do not provide a general criterion determining whether the trajectory visits or bypasses the gradient-descent stationary point. Moreover, without the additional assumption, the first stationary points reached by finite-depth Newton–Schulz dynamics and gradient descent may have the same loss. Such equal-loss behavior may reveal further dynamical structures, which we leave for future work. The rest of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 introduces the model and pathwise comparison criteria. Sections 3–5 establish the Gaussian entrance law, continuation criteria, and eventual depth guarantee. Section 6 presents an exact empirical task, and Section 7 discusses the scope of the results and open questions. Detailed proofs are given in the appendices.

In this paper, we have studied how finitely many iterations of a nonlinear matrix transformation can reshape optimization dynamics. In a quadratic two-layer network, we have characterized the evolution from small-initialization escape near the origin to the first nonzero stationary stage. Our results provide a precise description of how the number of Newton–Schulz iterations controls early rank selection and regulates the subsequent optimization path.
